appraisal_events.evidence: Mme de Villeparisis reports that Robert's family furiously resents the officer who granted the leave for Bruges, calling him 'quelqu'un de très mal... de très, très mal' and mockingly using his title 'le Prince de Borodino' as a Guermantes for whom the Empire does not count.
appraisal_events.explanation: The family, voiced through Mme de Villeparisis, harshly blames capitaine de Borodino for enabling Saint-Loup's affair, though the narrator frames her moral outrage and mocking use of his title as somewhat performative, an ironic 'accent vertueux' typical even of the most depraved Guermantes.

appraisal_events.evidence: Bloch praises well-bred people without realizing, being himself ill-bred, how displeasing his remarks are, then tells a long anecdote meant to impress that instead falls flat and remains incomprehensible to his listeners, since he mistakes Sir Rufus Israël for a prestigious figure when the Guermantes milieu regards him as a merely tolerated parvenu.
appraisal_events.explanation: Bloch's attempt to impress through anecdote and name-dropping backfires, exposing both his social tone-deafness and his misjudgment of what actually carries prestige in this milieu.

appraisal_events.evidence: Bloch cites as proof of Saint-Loup's perfect breeding that he introduced a young man simply, without exaggerated fuss and without any visible embarrassment.
appraisal_events.explanation: Within Bloch's otherwise misjudged anecdote, the underlying fact of Saint-Loup's unaffected, gracious manner toward someone he did not know to be wealthy stands as genuine local praise.

status_effects.explanation: He is harshly and explicitly condemned as morally very bad for enabling the affair.
His princely Napoleonic title is mockingly invoked and dismissed by a Guermantes for whom Empire-derived nobility does not truly count.
Bloch is shown as tactless and self-unaware, and his effort to impress with an anecdote collapses when his sense of what is prestigious proves badly mistaken.
The anecdote, despite Bloch's flawed framing, still credits Saint-Loup with genuine, unaffected good manners.

ambiguities: Mme de Villeparisis's moral condemnation of capitaine de Borodino is undercut by the narrator's aside that such virtuous tones are typical even of the most depraved Guermantes, so her blame is genuine within the family's view but not straightforwardly endorsed by the narrator.
